title: AI infrastructure and the neoclouds
lede: In the autumn of 2025, as combined hyperscaler capital-expenditure pledges for the year crested a quarter of a trillion dollars, a new investable category was crystallising around the AI buildout: the neocloud. Serenity committed more than $1.5 million to a ranked basket of GPU-rental platforms and miner-to-HPC pivots, framing the trade as a direct downstream play on hyperscaler overflow demand. By spring 2026 the cluster had gone quiet — not because the thesis was wrong, but because the discrimination within it had already been made.
body:
## The neocloud hypothesis

In late September 2025, Serenity posted what would become the cluster's founding document:

> The NeoCloud Thesis: Hyperscaler Capex Funnel. Why I'm putting $1.5M+ into Neoclouds, and why this might be a 200–300%+ return.

The bucket structure was revealing: “Mag7 contracts” covered CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius Group (NBIS), and Cipher Digital (CIFR); “with compute” captured IREN Limited (IREN) and bitcoin miners including Bitfarms; a third tier was labelled “speculative.” The thesis rested on a single mechanic — hundreds of billions in hyperscaler capital expenditure had to flow somewhere, and the *neoclouds* (GPU-specialist infrastructure providers that rent accelerator capacity rather than offering the broad service catalogues of Amazon, Microsoft (MSFT), or Google) sat closest to the tap.

## Margins over megawatts

Within five weeks the basket had been sorted. By end of October 2025 Serenity had begun separating the category into qualitatively different species:

> Markets are starting to price in a divergence between AWS-style full-stack Neoclouds like $NBIS and miners such as $CIFR, $BITF, $CLSK, and others. This is the reason I sold off $IREN $WULF and others, and consolidated into Nebius. Why? Margins > Capacity.

The distinction was between *full-stack* providers — combining GPU hardware with software orchestration, storage, and managed inference — and *capacity* plays: power-dense facilities with repurposed mining rigs or bare GPU racks. Nebius Group stood as the archetype of the former. The Amsterdam-headquartered successor to Yandex’s international operations, rebuilt after a $5.4 billion divestiture of Russian domestic assets in July 2024, had been reconstituted under co-founder Arkady Volozh with deep distributed-systems engineering and a full managed-inference stack. Serenity’s twelve-month price target of $400 rested on explicit margin arithmetic:

> $NBIS is the next Microsoft in the making. Scaling from $100M quarterly revenue to $2B–3B+ in 1–2 years off 55–75% gross margin. Large ownership of next-generational companies like ClickHouse. Infrastructure of Mag7 AI Compute. Completely undervalued.

**Nebius’s** subsequently reported results offered partial corroboration: full-year 2025 revenue of $529.8 million, up 479% year-on-year, with 2026 guidance of $3.0–3.4 billion. A reported $2.7 billion infrastructure agreement with Meta, if finalised, would represent a step-function expansion beyond its existing hyperscaler base.

## The CoreWeave sceptic

CoreWeave occupied an ambiguous position from the outset — listed in the “Mag7 contracts” bucket but attracting growing scepticism as the thesis matured. The company had gone public on NASDAQ on 28 March 2025 at $40 per share, and its commercial model — long-term, debt-financed GPU-capacity contracts, often three to seven years in duration, collateralised against the GPU hardware itself — drew an analogy from Serenity that became the cluster’s most-quoted formulation. When NVIDIA (NVDA) invested $2 billion in CoreWeave at $87.20 per share in January 2026, Serenity read the move sceptically:

> A casino gives you more money, so you could take on more debt with collateral to gamble. Then all the extra money goes back to the Casino (aka. $NVDA). That doesn’t make Coreweave a good long.

By the same week, the position had turned formally short:

> $CRWV is probably the only $50B+ company I can think of that is likely going to go bankrupt. At least $ORCL has a profitable core business and owns tons of assets. Coreweave is a clear short to me purely because a large part of their revenue will be used to…

The critique was structural rather than cyclical. CoreWeave’s model requires perpetual debt refinancing to fund hardware whose replacement cycle is measured in months; Microsoft accounted for approximately 67% of FY2025 revenue of $5.1 billion, leaving the business acutely exposed to a single customer that could in principle build its own capacity. **The bear thesis has yet to resolve.** CoreWeave priced a $3.5 billion convertible notes offering in April 2026, signed a multi-year capacity deal with Anthropic, and reported total remaining performance obligations implying roughly thirteen years of revenue at current run rates — each step deepening the symbiosis with NVIDIA that Serenity had identified as the structural trap.

## The IREN about-turn

IREN Limited, rebranded from Iris Energy in November 2024, was initially held as a “compute” neocloud on the thesis that a hyperscaler contract would follow its power infrastructure. One did: a $9.7 billion, five-year GPU hosting agreement with Microsoft for 76,000 NVIDIA GB300 processors at its Childress, Texas campus. But the terms of financing the pivot mattered more than the headline. When IREN launched a $6 billion *at-the-money* equity offering in March 2026 — nearly half its then-market capitalisation — the position was closed:

> I see zero compelling case to hold $IREN. Especially given the new $6B share dilution at a $12.8B marketcap. People will likely see that marketcap inflate to $20–25B. But the value of their shares decrease over time.

The episode crystallised a principle running through the entire cluster: capacity expansion funded by equity dilution transfers value from existing shareholders to the infrastructure buildout itself. Only operators with sufficient software margin — and thus access to non-dilutive convertible financing — can compound shareholder value through the cycle. IREN’s dossier reads “BEAR” in the xalpha data despite carrying 0.76 annualised alpha — a reminder that price appreciation and thesis conviction are separable.

## Power as the hidden bottleneck

The cluster’s energy and infrastructure names — Vistra (VST), Constellation Energy (CEG), Talen Energy (TLN), Vertiv (VRT), Digital Realty (DLR), and Equinix (EQIX) — received notably lighter treatment. Serenity was candid about the coverage gap:

> I’ve heard of $NEE and $CEG but I don’t know enough about energy. So I’m just half-blindly buying the sector from other DD I’ve seen.

The logic was nonetheless coherent. Nuclear generation — the only source that simultaneously satisfies AI *baseload* requirements and corporate carbon mandates — was accumulating long-dated *power-purchase agreements* (PPAs) at rates that made each incremental contract highly accretive to earnings. **Constellation Energy** (CEG), the largest US nuclear operator with 21,000 megawatts across 21 reactors, has signed 20-year PPAs with both Microsoft and Meta that lock in revenue through the 2050s. Vistra (VST) guided 2026 adjusted EBITDA to $6.8–7.6 billion — roughly $1 billion above its 2025 range — anchored by 2.6 gigawatts of nuclear output contracted to Meta for two decades. Vertiv, which supplies power conversion and thermal management equipment for hyperscale data centres, rounds out the energy-adjacent layer as a direct beneficiary of the load growth driving those PPAs without requiring a nuclear licence.

## Silence as signal

The cluster’s zero-call stretch in the four weeks to 8 May 2026, while Serenity’s photonics and advanced-packaging coverage remained active, most likely reflects portfolio consolidation rather than thesis abandonment. The original basket — 79 calls peaking at 55 between September and October 2025 — has been thinned through deliberate attrition: IREN exited in late October and actively shorted by implication in March; CoreWeave turned short in January; energy names were always sector exposures rather than high-conviction single-stock picks; and the *colocation* tier — Cipher Digital (CIFR), Core Scientific (CORZ), and Applied Digital (APLD), hyperscaler-leased facilities that do not own the GPUs they host — attracted measured rather than concentrated conviction. What remains implicit is a position in Nebius as the canonical full-stack neocloud: a wager that the engineering depth inherited from Yandex, combined with software-defined margins the pure capacity providers cannot replicate, will produce a materially different earnings trajectory as the buildout matures.

Whether that holds depends on whether hyperscaler demand remains structurally sticky — a question Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, framed with unusual candour in early 2026, warning that the industry faced “bankruptcy risk” if revenue growth failed to keep pace with capital expenditure. **The capex funnel Serenity identified in September 2025 is still flowing.** The question is whether the pipes at the downstream end are built to last.

concepts.definition: A GPU-specialist cloud provider that rents NVIDIA accelerator capacity to AI developers and research labs, sitting between the chip manufacturers and the frontier labs. Unlike the major hyperscalers, neoclouds do not offer a broad service catalogue; their value proposition is fast access to large volumes of GPU compute, often under long-term contracts.

A neocloud that goes beyond bare GPU rental to provide software orchestration, managed storage, inference endpoints, and developer tooling. The full-stack model generates higher gross margins than raw capacity provision because customers pay for software value on top of hardware, creating switching costs that pure capacity providers lack.

An infrastructure operator that provides raw compute or power-dense colocation facilities without a proprietary software layer, often a repurposed bitcoin miner. Capacity plays rely on hyperscaler lease agreements for revenue and are subject to dilutive equity offerings to fund capital expenditure, limiting compounding for existing shareholders.

The strategic reorientation of a cryptocurrency mining company toward high-performance computing and AI workloads. Miners have power infrastructure and data-centre facilities that can be redeployed to host AI GPUs; the pivot requires either purchasing GPUs directly or signing colocation agreements with hyperscalers who supply the hardware.

A long-term contract between a power generator and a buyer — typically a hyperscaler or data-centre operator — fixing the price and volume of electricity delivery over periods of 10–20 years. Nuclear PPAs are particularly sought after because they guarantee baseload, carbon-free power at predictable cost, satisfying both reliability and sustainability requirements for AI data centres.

A data-centre hosting model in which the facility operator provides power, space, and physical infrastructure while the customer — typically a hyperscaler — installs and owns the servers and networking equipment. Colocation operators earn lease income without bearing GPU ownership or replacement risk.

serenity_quotes_used.context: Founding neocloud thesis post: $1.5M+ commitment, 200–300% return target, bucket taxonomy of Mag7 contracts vs compute vs speculative
Divergence call: IREN and WULF sold, consolidated into NBIS; Margins > Capacity principle stated explicitly
NBIS bull thesis: next-Microsoft framing, 55–75% gross margin projection, ClickHouse ownership, Mag7 infrastructure claim
Casino analogy for CoreWeave/NVIDIA symbiosis; contra-CRWV thesis stated after NVDA equity investment announcement
Formal CRWV short call: bankruptcy thesis, structural debt critique, only $50B+ company likely to go bankrupt
IREN exit on $6B ATM dilution: dilution-value transfer principle stated; zero compelling case thesis
Energy sector admission: half-blind sector exposure rather than high-conviction single-name thesis on CEG/VST
